meta.label: Mid-range EN-B to high-end EN-B
meta.pilot_facing_title: Moving from a mid-B to a high-B
meta.intro: 32 questions, one tap each. This is one of the better-evidenced rungs on the ladder: several sources land on roughly the same amount of thermic flying before a high-B, and the makers of the best-known high-B wings all say much the same thing about who they're for. So the questions get more specific here than at the steps below, and more of them are about what you actually do in rough air than about your lifetime total. Answer honestly rather than optimistically — "not yet" and "nearly" are useful, normal answers, and they come with a list of what to work on.
meta.confidence_statement_for_ui: The guidance behind this step is firmer than for the rungs below it. Three sources land on roughly 50 hours of thermic flying, and three manufacturers independently describe their high-B wings as not for beginners or occasional pilots. One honest caveat: two of those three hours sources share an author, so treat the agreement as real but not quite as broad as it first looks. It's still a steer and a to-do list, not a clearance.
design_notes: CONFIDENCE. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md calls this "one of the stronger-consensus steps in the ladder" and that drove four concrete choices, not just tone. (a) The hours question that actually gates is a THERMIC-hours question, because all three hours sources measure thermic flying specifically, not cumulative total airtime — see 'thermic_airtime'. (b) Currency gets a combination gate of its own, on the strength of three manufacturer-via-retailer sources saying their high-B wings are not for occasional pilots. (c) The Ready-blocker list is longer here (10 questions) than at either step below, because more of the individual checks are genuinely sourced at this boundary. (d) The pilot-facing confidence statement above is positive but still names the independence caveat out loud.

INDEPENDENCE CAVEAT. knowledge/disagreements.md point 6 records that the Cross Country Magazine piece behind the ~50-hour figure is written by Greg Hamerton, who was Flybubble's long-time content lead. So the ~50-hour agreement is closer to two independent voices (a Hamerton/Flybubble house view, plus 406 Paragliding) than three. Nothing pilot-facing in this rubric claims three independent sources agree, and the gate on thermic hours is deliberately set well below the figure itself rather than at it.

HOURS IN BANDS, AND SPLIT FOUR WAYS. Per knowledge/disagreements.md point 2, cumulative hours, thermic hours, hours in the last 12 months and hours on the current wing are four separate questions with four separate weights, all in broad bands. The thermic question carries by far the most weight because it is the one the sources actually measure. paragliding24.ch's 50-80 ANNUAL hours band for high-B is used as the TOP of the airtime_last_12m scale, not as a bar to clear, because knowledge/disagreements.md point 6 flags that source's tidy ladder as uncorroborated.

SUB-CLASS FUZZINESS. Per knowledge/disagreements.md point 3, no question asks the pilot to classify their own wing as low/mid/high B, and no score depends on that label. This matters slightly less here than at the step below — Advance, Gin and Nova all do treat high-B as a distinct tier in their own positioning — but Niviuk still avoids the labels entirely, so they are used descriptively only.
NO NATIONAL RATING. Per knowledge/disagreements.md point 5, we never ask which pilot rating the pilot holds.

GROUND HANDLING. Asked, scored, never gated, and — as at the step below — not even a Ready-blocker. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source gives a ground-handling test for this step, and that BHPA's own Pilot Rating Scheme page was checked directly and doesn't name ground handling at all. The scale is raised to include Urs Aschmann's advanced drills, because he and Flybubble both treat kiting as the skill that teaches a pilot what a wing feels like just before it folds — which is exactly what this step's other sources expect in the air.

AMBITIONS. Carry no score at all, per knowledge/disagreements.md point 9. They do two jobs only: they combine with thin readiness in the 'ambition_without_readiness' gate, and they tell the rubric what air the pilot's own plans point at, which shapes which suggestions appear. Unlike at the two steps below, ambitions do NOT exempt any Ready-blocker at this step — see the 'no stated-plans exemption' note in config/scoring/mid-b-to-high-b.json. Both remaining uses are asymmetric in the conservative direction.

SIV. Optional, bonus-only, capped, can never subtract. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source treats SIV as a gate here. But knowledge/disagreements.md points 8 and 12 give this step a stronger claim on the SUGGESTION than any other: two independent experts (Hamerton on compounding risk, Simon Winkler on training feasibility) argue collapse-recovery training has to happen on lower-class wings, because wings from roughly EN-C up resist collapsing too well to simulate it realistically. A mid-B is one of the last wings a pilot will own where that training is genuinely representative, and the suggestion says so.

WHAT THE STEP IS REALLY TESTING. Three manufacturer-via-retailer sources (Advance, Gin, Nova) and Seb Ospina via XC Mag point the same way: this tier is for pilots who are current and who have already run out of wing, not for pilots who want more performance in the abstract. That is why 'wing_limiting_evidence' exists as its own question — it asks for Ospina's behavioural marker directly rather than inferring it from the motivation question.

ORDERED FLAGS. Questions marked "ordered": false are not a worst-to-best ladder and the UI must never imply the last option is the best one. At this step that covers thermalling (because "I mostly soar rather than thermal" is low-information, not bad), conditions flown, speed bar, collapse history, what your hands do, whether the wing has limited you, and all the motivation and mindset questions.

CHAIN MERGE (BRIEF.md 'Multi-step jumps'). app/upgrade/lib/mergeQuestions.ts only asks a question once across a chain when its id, text, option ids AND option labels are byte-identical. Twenty-three of the 32 questions here are byte-identical to their config/questions/low-b-to-mid-b.json counterparts and will merge into a single screen in a low-B to high-B run: ambitions, decline_to_fly, flying_frequency, incidents_12m, manoeuvre_course, peer_pressure, reserve_familiarity, response_when_rough, training_status, current_wing_time, ground_handling_practice, launch_reliability, thermal_turn_control, reading_the_day, active_piloting, conditions_flown, site_variety, collapse_experience, descent_options, upgrade_motivation, progress_goals, learning_curve_willingness, external_feedback. Each of those asks the same thing of the same pilot, with the same answer options meaning the same thing; only the SCORES attached to those options differ by step, which is exactly how per-leg scoring is meant to work. Where the merge key deliberately differs it is because the answer bands or the question genuinely change at this step: total_airtime, total_flights, airtime_last_12m (hours bands scale up), thermic_airtime (new question), ground_handling_kiting, speed_bar, collapse_practice (scales extended upward with this step's own sourced material), wing_limiting_evidence (new question) and wing_expectation (names the target class in its text). Help text is NOT part of the merge key, so several merged questions carry step-specific help here; in a chained run the pilot sees the earlier step's help, which is the existing behaviour for manoeuvre_course across the two steps below.

deliberately_not_asked: (1) Strongest thermal or conditions flown without a collapse. knowledge/disagreements.md point 7 records this was searched for specifically across every source and every step, found nowhere, and that the knowledge base recommends against inventing it — and knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md re-checked it at this boundary specifically, where sources do talk about turbulent thermic air in general terms, and still found nothing falsifiable. (2) Cross-country distance flown. knowledge/steps/mid-b-to-high-b.md records that no source ties an XC distance to this boundary (the numbers only appear one rung up, via pilot-rating ladders), and knowledge/disagreements.md point 14 adds a credible industry voice (Joy Paragliding) arguing distance is a poor proxy for wing readiness anyway. (3) Which sub-class the current wing is — see the sub-class note above. (4) Whether the pilot has done an SIV course is asked, but is outside the scored set — bonus only. Each of these is an absence in the research, not an oversight, and is recorded here so a later reviewer does not 'fix' it by adding an unsourced question.

sections.title: On the ground and on launch

questions.text: Roughly how many hours have you flown in total, since you started?
questions.help: A rough band is fine. Count solo airtime, not tandems. The next question matters more than this one at this step.

options.label: Under 50 hours
Between 50 and 100 hours
Between 100 and 200 hours
More than 200 hours

questions.text: Roughly how many flights have you done altogether?
questions.help: No source puts a flight count on this particular step, so this counts for very little — it's here because flights and hours tell you different things.

options.label: Fewer than 75
Between 75 and 150
Between 150 and 300
More than 300

questions.text: And roughly how many of those hours have been in thermic air?
questions.help: Thermal flying, not ridge or coastal soaring and not evening glass-offs. This is the number the guidance for this step actually measures, so it's worth a moment's honest thought. If most of your airtime is ridge soaring, one source counts that at roughly half the value of thermic time.

options.label: Under 10 hours
Between 10 and 25 hours
Between 25 and 50 hours
Between 50 and 100 hours
More than 100 hours

questions.text: How many hours have you flown in the last 12 months?
questions.help: Asked separately on purpose. The makers of the best-known high-B wings all say much the same thing — these aren't wings for occasional pilots — so how much you're flying now carries real weight here.

options.label: Under 10 hours
Between 10 and 25 hours
Between 25 and 50 hours
Between 50 and 80 hours
More than 80 hours

questions.text: How many hours have you flown on the wing you're on now?
questions.help: The wing you'd be replacing.

options.label: Under 20 hours
Between 20 and 50 hours
Between 50 and 100 hours
More than 100 hours

questions.text: Where are you with your training?

options.label: Still in training, or still flying under instructor supervision
Qualified fairly recently and starting to fly on my own
Qualified a while ago and flying independently

questions.text: Over the last three months, how often have you actually got in the air?
questions.help: Think about months with flyable weather, not the whole calendar.

options.label: I haven't flown at all in the last three months
Less than once a month
About once a month
Two or three times a month
About once a week or more

questions.text: How far have you taken your ground handling?
questions.help: No source sets a ground-handling bar for this particular step — we checked the official UK pilot-rating pages directly and they don't mention it at all. So this is information rather than a test you can fail.

options.label: It still gets away from me on a breezy day
I can hold it steady overhead and walk around under it
Confident in stronger wind — I can turn it, put it where I want and kill it quickly
All that, plus harder drills — one-sided inflations, rear-riser control, feeling the pressure change before it folds

questions.text: How often do you practise with the wing on the ground, away from flying?

options.label: Never — I only handle the wing when I'm about to fly
Hardly ever
Now and then, when a day's unflyable
Regularly, as its own thing

questions.text: How reliable are your launches, and in how wide a range of conditions?
questions.help: Count forward and reverse. The thing that moves this answer is the range of conditions, not just the success rate at your home site.

options.label: Not that reliable — I regularly need several goes, get pulled around, or abort
Clean first time about half the time
Nearly always clean, but only on the sites and days I know well
Nearly always clean, in the conditions I choose to fly
Reliable across a fair range — stronger wind, some cross, slopes I haven't launched before

questions.text: How are you with turning in a thermal?
questions.help: There's no wrong answer, including the last one — plenty of people fly happily without thermalling much.

options.label: Not confident with it yet
I can climb in wide, gentle turns, but I lose the core easily
I can centre a climb and change bank angle deliberately, turning both ways
That, plus I'm comfortable in a busy thermal and can tighten up when the core is small
I mostly soar or glide rather than thermal, so this hasn't really come up

questions.text: How well can you read how a day is going to develop?
questions.help: Wind, gradient, where and when the thermals will work, when it'll get strong, when to be somewhere else.

options.label: I mostly go when other people say it's good — I couldn't really call it myself
I have a go at reading it and I'm right about half the time
I can usually tell how it'll develop and when to be careful
I plan my flying around how the day will build, and I'm rarely caught out

questions.text: When the air gets bumpy, what do your hands actually do?

options.label: They stop moving — I hold still and wait it out
I grip the brakes and pull them in a bit
I try to react, but it's not automatic yet
I work the brakes to keep the pressure even and the wing overhead
That's automatic now, and my hands sit differently depending on what the air's doing

questions.text: What kind of air have you been flying in, mostly?

options.label: Smooth evenings and calm mornings, mostly
Ridge and coastal soaring, not much thermic
Light to moderate thermals
Proper thermic days, fairly regularly
Strong thermic or big mountain days, fairly regularly

questions.text: How many different sites have you flown?
questions.help: Low confidence on this one — it comes from the French training ladder rather than from anything written about wing classes, so it counts for very little here.

options.label: Pretty much just my home site
Two or three, all fairly similar
Several, including different types — coastal, inland, mountain
I fly somewhere new fairly regularly and I'm comfortable working a site out

questions.text: How do you use the speed bar?
questions.help: More isn't automatically better, and how you put it on matters as much as how much you use. This is the first step where the bar is described as a normal cross-country tool rather than an occasional extra.

options.label: I've never really used it
I've tried it gently, in smooth air with plenty of height
I use it to get out of sinking air, and otherwise leave it alone
A bit of bar on most glides, easing on and off as the wing moves
On bar for most of my gliding — I ease it on watching the pitch, trim the pressure to keep the wing settled, and come off it when the air changes
I push it on quickly when I want the speed, including fairly low down

questions.text: Has the wing collapsed on you in flight, and what happened?
questions.help: "Never" is still a normal answer and isn't counted against you.

options.label: Never
Small tip collapses that sorted themselves out
Something bigger — around half the wing — and I caught it and flew it out
Yes, and I froze; the wing recovered on its own, not because of me
Yes, and it got away from me — I lost control of where the wing was going
It's happened a few times and I still struggle to sort it out

questions.text: How much have you practised collapses, wingovers and spirals deliberately?
questions.help: Not a trick question. The guidance for this step asks for this as regular practice rather than something you've read about — and the wing you're on now is one of the last you'll own where a collapse can be made to behave realistically.

options.label: Not at all — I'd be working it out for the first time
I know in theory what to do, but I've never practised it
I've pulled and released tip folds myself, with plenty of height
I practise wingovers, spirals and asymmetrics fairly regularly
I've worked on all of that with an instructor or on a course, and I keep it current

questions.text: If you needed to come down quickly, what could you actually do?

options.label: Big ears, but I'm not that confident with them
Big ears, comfortably
Big ears plus one other way down I've actually used
Ears, bigger tip folds and a controlled spiral — all practised

questions.text: Your reserve — where is it, and have you ever practised the throw?

options.label: I'm not completely sure I could find the handle in a hurry
I know exactly where the handle is, but I've never practised
I've practised the throw at least once, hanging in a harness
Practised recently, and the repack is up to date

questions.text: Have you done a manoeuvres course (over water, with an instructor)?
questions.help: Optional, and no source makes one a requirement at this step. It can only help your result here, never hurt it — though two instructors argue separately that if you're ever going to do one, the wing you own now is close to the best one to do it on.

options.label: No
Not yet, but I've got one booked
Yes, one
Yes, more than one

questions.text: Has your current wing actually been the thing that stopped you doing something?
questions.help: The most useful question on this page, and the one it's easiest to answer generously. Think about specific flights rather than a general feeling.

options.label: Not really — I don't think the wing has held me back yet
I've wondered, but I couldn't point to a particular flight
Yes — I get left behind on glides by people on higher-class wings
Yes — I can name flights where I couldn't get back or couldn't cross something, and more glide would have done it
Regularly — I'm flying at the edge of what it has to give on most cross-country days

questions.text: What's the main reason you want to move up?
questions.help: Pick the one closest to the truth, not the one that sounds best. Wanting more performance is a completely normal answer and isn't marked down.

options.label: I've got everything out of my current wing that it has to give
My instructor or coach suggested it
I want more glide and speed for longer flights
I need a new wing anyway, so I may as well go a step up
Most of the people I fly with are on something higher and I don't want to be the odd one out
I'm hoping a better wing will cope with conditions I currently find hard

questions.text: What do you expect to actually change on a high-B?

options.label: A bit more glide and speed — honestly, not a huge difference
More feedback, more pitch to manage, and more to do when it's rough
I'm not really sure — I haven't looked into it
Flying will feel less like hard work than it does now
It'll handle turbulence better than my current wing

questions.text: What are you mainly trying to get better at this season?

options.label: Flying more smoothly, staying relaxed when it's rough, enjoying it more
Specific skills — centring climbs, launches, reading the day
Flying further and getting my distances up
Keeping up with, or ahead of, the people I fly with
I haven't really thought about it in those terms

questions.text: A new wing means a spell of relearning it — ground handling, launches, how it talks to you. How does that sit with you?

options.label: Fine — I'd spend time on the ground with it before flying anything demanding
Fine — I'd keep to easy days and familiar sites for a while
I'd rather just get on and fly it
I'd expect to be straight back to normal on it within a flight or two

questions.text: Over the next year, what kind of flying do you mainly want to be doing?
questions.help: Pick any that apply, including things you're only thinking about. There's no better or worse answer here — it doesn't add or lose you any points. It tells us which skills your own plans will actually ask of you, so the advice fits the flying you do.

options.label: Local flying, ridge or coastal soaring
Cross-country flights — first ones, or building them up
Long cross-country flights
Hike and fly in the mountains
Competitions
Acro or wing-overs
Nothing in particular — just enjoying it

questions.text: Has anyone who has actually watched you fly said anything about moving up?

options.label: An instructor or coach has told me to wait
Nobody who knows what they're looking at has seen me fly lately
Flying mates reckon I'd be fine on one
An instructor or coach has said I'm ready

questions.text: When the air gets properly rough, what usually happens for you?
questions.help: Everyone's heart rate goes up. We're asking what you do next.

options.label: I lock up a bit — I hang on and wait for it to pass
I get tense, want to land straight away, and my flying gets scrappier
Heart rate goes up, but I carry on flying the wing
I stay fairly calm, keep flying actively, and have a way out if it builds
It doesn't really bother me

questions.text: In the last few months, have you walked away from a launch, or landed early, because the day wasn't what you wanted to handle?

options.label: More than once, and I was happy with the call
Once or twice
No — I generally launch and see how it goes
No — it hasn't come up

questions.text: Your friends are launching into a day you're unsure about. What usually happens?

options.label: I go too — I don't want to be the one left on the hill
I feel the pull, but I usually wait
I make my own call and I'm comfortable either way
Hasn't come up

questions.text: In the last 12 months, any incidents or near misses? A messy launch, a hard landing, a scare in the air?
questions.help: Nobody sees this but you. An honest answer makes the result worth having.

options.label: Nothing I'd call a near miss
One or two moments that made me think — and I know what I'd do differently
A few, and I'm not really sure what went wrong
Something that shook me up, and I've been uneasy flying since
An injury, or I threw my reserve
